finding.title: Algorithm confusion: asymmetric key material classified as HMAC secret enables JWT forgery
finding.evidence: Attacker input: a JWT whose header is {"alg":"HS256"} and whose signature is HMAC-SHA256 over header.payload computed with the victim's *public* key bytes as the HMAC secret (the key material is public, so the attacker can compute it). Flow: createVerifier({key}) (no algorithms, or algorithms derived from the key) reaches verifier.js:401 `detectPublicKeyAlgorithms(key)`; in performDetectPublicKeyAlgorithms the public key is only recognised when the '^'-anchored publicKeyPemMatcher matches at offset 0, and the certificate branch only checks key.includes('-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----'). Any asymmetric key that is not a bare PEM matching those exact patterns — e.g. PEM with a leading byte (newline/space/zero-width char) or a serialized public JWK/JWKS JSON — fails both checks, so control falls to line 133-135 `else if (!publicKeyPemMatch && !key.includes(publicKeyX509CertMatcher)) return hsAlgorithms`. verifier.js:406 then assigns allowedAlgorithms = ['HS256','HS384','HS512'] and verifier.js:409 builds an HMAC secret from the same bytes via prepareKeyOrSecret(key, true). Because verifySignature's HS branch (crypto.js:282-284) computes HMAC over `input` with that key and compares timing-safely, the forged HS256 token verifies, bypassing the RSA/EC public-key signature that the caller intended. The public-key/secret distinction is never enforced against the key type, only against fragile string patterns, so no protection stops the symmetric fallback. PoC executed locally with this source: a token signed HS256 using a leading-newline public PEM was ACCEPTED ({"sub":"admin","role":"admin"}) while the identical token against the un-prefixed PEM was rejected FAST_JWT_INVALID_ALGORITHM; a token signed with a public JWK JSON string as secret was likewise ACCEPTED by createVerifier({key: jwkJson}). Reachable identically through the async-key path at verifier.js:342/344 where the returned key is auto-classified.

review_queue.evidence: Claimed HS256 algorithm confusion when PEM key material is not matched at offset 0. The detection path and a working forgery were not reproduced; keep unreviewed.

finding.title: Algorithm confusion: public asymmetric JWK/JSON key misclassified as HMAC secret
finding.evidence: Attacker input: a JWT whose header sets alg to HS256 plus the server public key material. Flow: createVerifier classifies options.key via detectPublicKeyAlgorithms(key) (src/verifier.js:401) and, on the raw-secret branch, calls prepareKeyOrSecret(key, availableAlgorithms[0] === hsAlgorithms[0]) (src/verifier.js:409), producing an HMAC secret; verifyToken then validates the signature with HMAC at src/verifier.js:139 (verifySignature(header.alg, key, input, signature)). In performDetectPublicKeyAlgorithms (src/crypto.js:125-136) the only asymmetric-key recognition is the ^-anchored PEM regexes on lines 126/128/130. A serialized public JWK, for example a JSON object with kty RSA plus n and e, matches none of them, so control falls through to the Not a PEM, assume a plain secret branch and returns hsAlgorithms at line 135. The verifier then treats that public JSON string as an HMAC secret, and any attacker who knows the public-by-design JWK can compute HMAC-SHA256 over the signing input and be accepted as an authenticated token (alg confusion / signature forgery). Failed protection: the same file in the upstream released fast-jwt 5.0.0 contains explicit guards (isAsymmetricJwkJson and assertNotAsymmetricJwkJson) that throw FAST_JWT_INVALID_KEY for raw RSA/EC/OKP JWK JSON; this target build removed them and the verifier still routes JWK material through prepareKeyOrSecret without any asymmetric-JSON rejection. Required configuration: verifier key supplied as raw JWK or JWKS JSON, a documented way to pass public keys, which is exactly the input the removed guard protected.

review_queue.evidence: Algorithm-family fallback in the HMAC-confusion family; not reproduced this round.

finding.title: Algorithm confusion: leading bytes before PEM header bypass asymmetric-key detection
finding.evidence: Attacker input: attacker-chosen HS256 JWT; server key is an asymmetric public or private PEM carrying any leading data. Flow: createVerifier calls detectPublicKeyAlgorithms(key) (src/verifier.js:401) which reaches performDetectPublicKeyAlgorithms (src/crypto.js:125). The matchers publicKeyPemMatcher and privateKeyPemMatcher (src/crypto.js:26-28) are ^-anchored, and line 133 treats the key as a raw secret whenever key.match(publicKeyPemMatcher) is falsy and the X509 certificate marker is absent. Any leading byte (whitespace, newline, control character, BOM, zero-width unicode, wrapper text) moves the BEGIN header off offset 0, so the asymmetric PEM is classified under Not a PEM, assume a plain secret and hsAlgorithms is returned at line 135. prepareKeyOrSecret (src/verifier.js:409) then builds an HMAC secret, and the signature check at src/verifier.js:139 verifies HMAC instead of RSA/EC, so a token forged by HMAC-ing the signing input with the full public PEM text as the secret is accepted. Failed protection: this build has no normalization or unanchored PEM search, whereas upstream fast-jwt 5.0.0 replaces the anchored matching with locatePem (unanchored BEGIN header search) plus explicit rejection of junk-prefixed PEM; that mitigation was removed here. Required configuration: key passed as a PEM string that carries at least one leading character before the BEGIN header.

review_queue.evidence: Claimed HS256 algorithm confusion when PEM key material is not matched at offset 0. The detection path and a working forgery were not reproduced; keep unreviewed.

finding.title: ThinVec::clear loses panic safety, leading to double free of elements
finding.evidence: `clear` runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` (line 1084) and only afterwards `self.set_len(0)` (line 1085) without any drop guard. If any element's `Drop::drop` panics while the slice is being dropped, unwinding skips `set_len(0)`, so the header `_len` still reports the old length while some elements have already had their destructors run and been logically consumed. The vector is then left with a stale length pointing at partially-dropped elements; a later `Drop for ThinVec` (line 1917 `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])`) or any `as_slice`/index/`clear`/`truncate` re-runs destructors on those already-dropped elements (double free / use-after-free / type-confusion). The attacker reaches this whenever attacker-influenced data flows into a `T::drop` that can panic (e.g. a destructor that panics on malformed input) in a program that unwinds (normal `catch_unwind`, or Gecko's nsTArray FFI where Rust destructors unwind into C++). Protections are insufficient because the only invariant-restoring write is placed after the fallible drop with no `DropGuard`; the upstream fix in thin-vec 0.2.16 adds exactly such a guard around this block, confirming this is the vulnerable site. Diff of the audited 0.2.15 source against 0.2.16 shows line 1084-1085 replaced by a `DropGuard` whose drop calls `self.0.set_len(0)`.

review_queue.evidence: clear drops its slice at 1084 before setting len to zero at 1085, so a destructor panic leaves a stale live length that a later drop re-drops. reference/FIX.md independently patches this path; distinct from IntoIter cleanup.

finding.title: IntoIter::drop loses panic safety, leading to double free of remaining elements
finding.evidence: `IntoIter::drop`'s inner `drop_non_singleton` replaces the iterator's vector with a fresh `ThinVec` (`let mut vec = mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new())`), then calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` (line 2547) before resetting the length with `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (line 2548), with no drop guard. If an element's `Drop::drop` panics during this `drop_in_place`, unwinding skips `set_len_non_singleton(0)` and the local `vec` is itself dropped during unwind: `ThinVec::drop` calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` (line 1917) on the same buffer, re-dropping the already-dropped elements (including the one whose destructor panicked) — a double free / use-after-free. An attacker triggers this by draining/iterating a `ThinVec` whose element destructor panics based on attacker-controlled state in an unwinding program, causing an exploitable double-free/heap corruption. The check `!self.vec.is_singleton()` at line 2552 does not help: the corrupting re-drop happens on the moved-out `vec` local inside `drop_non_singleton`. The 0.2.16 upstream fix replaces this body with a `DropGuard` that calls `self.0.vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` on unwind, confirming this exact line is the unguarded unsafe operation.

review_queue.evidence: IntoIter::drop drops its tail before zeroing len, so a destructor panic drops the stale local vector again. Same expected root cause at the adjacent unsafe operation.

finding.title: Double drop of items if their Drop panics during ThinVec::clear
finding.evidence: Safe API `ThinVec::clear` (line 1082) runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` (line 1084) BEFORE it resets the length with `self.set_len(0)` (line 1085). An item type whose `Drop` impl panics (a normal, safe scenario during cleanup) makes `drop_in_place` unwind after some elements have already been dropped; the `set_len(0)` on line 1085 is skipped, so the ThinVec still reports its original `len`. When the container is subsequently dropped (or unwound through) the destructor runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` again over the same, already-dropped elements and frees them a second time (a double free / use-after-free for `Box`/`String`-like items). There is no panic guard or early length update to make this unwind-safe. Upstream fixed exactly this in 0.2.16: release notes state 'Fix two double-drop issues with ThinVec::clear() and ThinVec::into_iter() when the Drop implementation of the item panics', and 0.2.21's `clear` now uses a DropGuard that decrements `len` 'even in the case of a panic'. Trigger: safe code pushes panic-on-drop values into a ThinVec and calls `clear()` (or drops the vec while unwinding).

review_queue.evidence: clear drops its slice at 1084 before setting len to zero at 1085, so a destructor panic leaves a stale live length that a later drop re-drops. reference/FIX.md independently patches this path; distinct from IntoIter cleanup.

finding.title: Double drop of moved-out/partially-dropped items in IntoIter::drop when an element Drop panics
finding.evidence: `IntoIter::drop` (line 2541) calls `drop_non_singleton` (line 2544), which does `let mut vec = mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new()); ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..]);` (lines 2546-2547). If one of the remaining elements' `Drop` panics, `ptr::drop_in_place` unwinds; the local `vec` (still carrying the FULL original length, because `set_len_non_singleton(0)` on line 2548 never ran) is then dropped by the unwinder. That second drop re-drops (a) elements already moved out and returned by earlier `next()` calls (`[0, start)`) and (b) the elements already destroyed in the failing `drop_in_place`, i.e. a double free. Note `next()` (line 2510) only `ptr::read`s and advances `start` without ever updating `vec.len()`, so the length always overstates the live elements. Trigger from safe code: `let it = v.into_iter(); it.next(); drop(it);` where a remaining element's destructor panics. Upstream 0.2.16 fixed this as one of its 'two double-drop issues ... when the Drop implementation of the item panics'; 0.2.21 wraps the drop in a DropGuard that resets the length during unwind.

review_queue.evidence: IntoIter::drop drops its tail before zeroing len, so a destructor panic drops the stale local vector again. Same expected root cause at the adjacent unsafe operation.

finding.title: Layout constructed with unchecked size/align can violate Layout invariant (invalid layout passed to allocator)
finding.evidence: `layout::<T>(cap)` (line 440) builds the allocator layout with `Layout::from_size_align_unchecked(alloc_size::<T>(cap), alloc_align::<T>())` (line 441). `alloc_size` (line 386) only guarantees the raw size is <= isize::MAX; it does not check that the size rounded up to `alloc_align` stays <= isize::MAX, which is a required invariant of `Layout`/`from_size_align_unchecked`. For an element type whose size is not a multiple of the header alignment (e.g. `T = u8`, where `alloc_align::<T>() = max(align_of::<u8>(), align_of::<Header>()) = 8`), calling the safe `ThinVec::<u8>::with_capacity(isize::MAX - size_of::<Header>())` makes `alloc_size` return exactly isize::MAX (0x7FFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF); rounding that up to alignment 8 overflows isize, so the constructed `Layout` is invalid and is then passed to `header_with_capacity` -> `alloc(layout)` (line 453) / `realloc` (line 1737), which is undefined behavior (in practice an overly-large/invalid allocation). The validation is bypassed by using the `_unchecked` constructor; upstream 0.2.19 replaced it with the checked `Layout::from_size_align(...).unwrap_cap_overflow()` and added regression test `test_cap_plus_header_rounded_up_overflows`.

review_queue.evidence: Rounded-size Layout requirement with an enormous capacity; project low-impact tuning case.

finding.title: Unvalidated nb_blocks causes heap out-of-bounds write in argon2i_32
finding.evidence: argon2i_32 passes the caller-supplied nb_blocks directly into the Argon2 config (line 328 `config.nb_blocks = nb_blocks`, with config.nb_lanes fixed to 1 at line 330) and allocates the work area from that same unvalidated value at line 345 (`malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * 1024)`). In monocypher.c:crypto_argon2 the internal geometry is derived as `segment_size = config.nb_blocks / config.nb_lanes / 4; lane_size = segment_size*4; nb_blocks = lane_size*config.nb_lanes;` so any nb_blocks < 4 yields segment_size = 0 and lane_size = 0. The block-initialization loop then unconditionally writes two 1024-byte blocks per lane (`blocks[l * lane_size + i]` for i in {0,1}), i.e. 2048 bytes starting at the base pointer, into a `malloc(0)` allocation, and later reads `last_block = blocks + lane_size - 1` = blocks-1. The Python wrapper performs no lower-bound (or >=8*nb_lanes) validation on nb_blocks before the call, so a caller passing e.g. nb_blocks=0,1,2,3 reaches crypto_argon2 with a zero-length buffer and is written out of bounds (heap corruption / crash). The only length checks in the wrapper are _validate_u32 on password/salt/key/ad sizes (lines 334-342), which do not constrain nb_blocks; the uint32 cast of config.nb_blocks on assignment also truncates the value while malloc uses the full Python integer, allowing further size/geometry mismatches for large values.

review_queue.evidence: crypto_argon2 is called with the caller-sized work area; same undersized-work-area root cause as the expected line-345 sink.

finding.title: Unchecked malloc result dereferenced by crypto_argon2
finding.evidence: Line 345 stores `work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * (<size_t> 1024))` but the return value is never checked for NULL. The value is then unconditionally passed to `crypto_argon2` at line 347, whose first action is to treat work_area as the Argon2 block array and write the initial blocks (`blocks[l * lane_size + i]`). A caller controlling nb_blocks can force a large allocation (the value is taken straight from the attacker-supplied argument with no upper bound), making malloc fail and return NULL; crypto_argon2 then dereferences the NULL pointer and writes to it. The try/finally only guarantees free() runs, not that the pointer is valid.

review_queue.evidence: malloc at line 345 is unchecked before crypto_argon2 consumes work_area at 347; a failed allocation dereferences NULL. Distinct availability failure from a successfully sized undersized allocation; OOM was not executed.

finding.title: Missing key/nonce length validation in lock/unlock/chacha20 causes out-of-bounds reads
finding.evidence: The module-level `lock` (line 166), `unlock` (line 185) and `chacha20` (line 257) accept key and nonce without checking their lengths before handing them to the C routines. `lock` calls `crypto_aead_lock(...)` at line 181 and `unlock` calls `crypto_aead_unlock(...)` at line 199; both C functions declare `const uint8_t key[32]` and `const uint8_t nonce[24]` and read those fixed sizes unconditionally. Unlike IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption (which validates len(key)==32 at line 214 and len(nonce)==24 at line 217) and elligator_map/elligator_rev, these free functions perform no such validation, so a caller passing a short key or nonce buffer (e.g. key=b'x') causes the C code to read up to 31/23 bytes past the end of the Python buffer. chacha20 only validates the nonce length (lines 266-272) and never the key length before crypto_chacha20_x/djb read the 32-byte key, giving an out-of-bounds read of adjacent memory that can be reflected through the resulting keystream.

review_queue.evidence: lock()/unlock() pass caller-controlled key and nonce buffers into native routines declaring key[32]/nonce[24] without a length check; the incremental wrapper guards lengths at lines 214-218. Distinct AEAD bounds defect; no native crash or disclosure reproduced.

finding.title: Unvalidated Blake2b key length causes stack buffer overflow
finding.evidence: blake2b() passes an arbitrary caller-supplied key to crypto_blake2b_keyed(hash, 64, key, len(key), msg, len(msg)) with no length check (line 281); Blake2b.__init__ has the same defect at line 297. The C function crypto_blake2b_keyed_init copies key_size bytes of the key into the fixed-size stack buffer `u8 key_block[128]` (monocypher.c:545-546, COPY is a byte-loop macro at monocypher.c:65). A key longer than 128 bytes overflows key_block and corrupts adjacent stack memory. The Cython signature `const uint8_t* key` accepts bytes of any length, so an attacker who controls the key only needs to call, e.g., monocypher.blake2b(b'msg', b'A'*512) (or Blake2b(key=b'A'*512)). No length validation, clamping, or error path exists in the wrapper.

review_queue.evidence: blake2b passes unbounded len(key) into crypto_blake2b_keyed; monocypher.c copies key_size bytes into key_block[128]. Keys >128 bytes overflow the stack. Source-verified; remote reachability is not claimed.

finding.title: Unvalidated Argon2 nb_blocks causes undersized work_area and heap overflow
finding.evidence: argon2i_32 accepts an attacker-controlled nb_blocks and uses it directly: config.nb_blocks = nb_blocks (line 328, no _validate_u32 / no lower bound) and work_area = malloc((size_t)nb_blocks * 1024) (line 345, return value unchecked). Monocypher requires nb_blocks >= 8*nb_lanes, which is never enforced. With nb_blocks=1 the wrapper allocates only 1024 bytes, but crypto_argon2 unconditionally writes two blocks per lane at the initialization loop `load64_le_buf(blocks[l*lane_size + i].a, ...)` for i=0,1 (monocypher.c:776-783); because segment_size=1/1/4=0, lane_size=0, blocks[1] lies one full 1024-byte block past the allocation, producing a 1024-byte heap out-of-bounds write. nb_blocks=0 additionally calls malloc(0). Reachable directly as monocypher.argon2i_32(1, 1, b'pw', b'salt').

review_queue.evidence: Unvalidated nb_blocks sizes the work area while native Argon2 reads initialized blocks; same expected undersized-work-area root cause with an alternate CWE at the expected line.

finding.title: Missing key/nonce/public-key length validation causes out-of-bounds reads
finding.evidence: Cryptographic wrapper functions declare fixed-size C array parameters (key[32], nonce[24], public_key[32], signature[64]) but never validate the Python input lengths before passing them to C. key_exchange() calls crypto_x25519(p, your_secret_key, their_public_key) (line 375) with no checks; Cython converts the bytes objects to raw pointers without enforcing the declared lengths, and crypto_x25519/crypto_x25519_public_key read full 32-byte operands (monocypher.c:1546-1561), so short inputs cause reads past the end of the bytes buffers. The same missing-validation pattern affects lock (line 181), unlock (line 199), chacha20 (key unchecked, lines 267-269), compute_key_exchange_public_key (line 362), and signature_check (line 429, reads a 64-byte signature and 32-byte public key). Reachable, e.g., as monocypher.key_exchange(b'\x01', b'\x02') or monocypher.signature_check(b'x', b'y', b'm'). Note the IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption class does check key/nonce lengths (lines 214-218), so the checks are simply absent from these module-level functions.

review_queue.evidence: key_exchange forwards caller-controlled fixed-size buffers without length validation; same wrapper bounds family as the promoted cases.

finding.title: ChunkedReader silently discards 2 arbitrary bytes after each chunk instead of validating the CRLF terminator, enabling HTTP request smuggling
finding.evidence:
Attacker-controlled chunked body bytes reach ChunkedReader.__call__ through Connection.receive_data -> next_event -> _extract_next_receive_event (h11/_connection.py:352-424) once the framing is chosen as "chunked" (h11/_connection.py:115-118, requiring Transfer-Encoding: chunked). After the final byte of a chunk is consumed (line 195, `self._bytes_in_chunk -= len(data)`), line 197 sets `self._bytes_to_discard = 2` and the next invocation takes the branch at lines 163-171, which does `data = buf.maybe_extract_at_most(self._bytes_to_discard)` and simply subtracts the length consumed: `self._bytes_to_discard -= len(data)`. The extracted bytes are never compared against the mandated CRLF chunk terminator (RFC 7230 section 4.1 requires `chunk = chunk-size [ chunk-ext ] CRLF chunk-data CRLF`). Thus a body such as `1
aXX1
b
0

` is accepted: `a` is emitted as data and the arbitrary bytes `XX` are discarded as if they were the chunk footer. The only validation applied to chunk framing is the chunk-size header regex (h11/_abnf.py:112-132, `validate(chunk_header_re, ...)` at h11/_readers.py:177-182), which does not constrain the post-data terminator. Consequently h11 accepts malformed chunks that a stricter front-end/proxy/backend parser will frame differently, so the two parsers disagree on message boundaries (request smuggling), letting an attacker smuggle a second request or poison the next request/response on a reused connection. Upstream fixed exactly this in h11 0.15.0 by replacing the integer counter with a literal tracker plus a comparison (`self._bytes_to_discard = b"
"`, and `if data != self._bytes_to_discard[:len(data)]: raise LocalProtocolError("malformed chunk footer ...")`); a direct diff of the target file (h11 0.14.0) against the fixed 0.16.0 h11/_readers.py shows the vulnerable branch is present only in the audited version (lines 163-171 and 197), confirming the missing protection rather than intended leniency. A local PoC script exercising h11.Connection(h11.SERVER) with the malformed body above was written to /tmp/poc.py, but no Python interpreter was reachable in the audit shell (the run produced no output), so the finding rests on the inspected source and the upstream fix diff, not on executed runtime output.

review_queue.evidence: The footer-discard branch is the alternate sink of the expected chunked-framing root cause.

finding.title: Negative block index (inBlockIndex-1) bypasses selector bounds check, forcing SHA-256 output to zero
finding.evidence: In Sha256General (and Sha256Partial line 292) the output block is selected with `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1;` (sha.circom:195). `inBlockIndex` is derived at sha.circom:110-111 only by `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9); paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512;`, which constrains paddedInLength to be a multiple of 512 but never constrains `inBlockIndex >= 1`. paddedInLength is an attacker-chosen input; the only bound is bitLengthVerifier (sha.circom:125-128) which accepts paddedInLength = 0. With paddedInLength = 0 the constraint gives inBlockIndex = 0, so index = -1, i.e. the field element p-1. ItemAtIndex's protection (array.circom:24-28) is `LessThan(bitLength)` comparing index against maxArrayLen; because index = p-1 the Num2Bits value `index + 2^bitLength - maxArrayLen` wraps modulo p to a small integer whose top bit is 0, so the check `lessThan.out === 1` PASSES even though -1 is not a valid index (verified numerically: for maxBlocks in {1,2,4,8}, index=-1 yields bound-check out=1 with no eq match). Every IsEqual in array.circom:35-41 then evaluates to 0 and CalculateTotal returns 0, so all 256 output bits become 0. The circuit is therefore satisfiable for an arbitrary `paddedIn` with `paddedInLength = 0` while claiming `out = 0x000...0`, which is not the real SHA-256 of any message (SHA-256 is never all-zero), breaking proof soundness — a malicious prover can forge a valid proof that a chosen padded input hashes to zero. The commented-out floor verifiers (sha.circom:114-122) and the numeric test also show the length verifier can be bypassed with a near-p value, but the reachable unsafe operation is the unguarded `inBlockIndex - 1` selector index at line 195.

review_queue.evidence: Unconstrained inBlockIndex derived from an unbounded paddedInLength reaches the ItemAtIndex selector. Same comparator/selector soundness defect as the expected line-126 sink.

finding.title: Out-of-range block index in SHA256 output selection lets a prover force the hash output to zero
finding.evidence: Sha256General/Sha256Partial derive the block selector index from the prover-supplied length: `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9); paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512;` (sha.circom:110-111 and 233-234), then assign `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1;` (sha.circom:195 and 292). The only constraints on paddedInLength are the upper-bound checks `bitLengthVerifier = LessEqThan(maxBitsPaddedBits); ... .out === 1` (sha.circom:125-128 / 237-240); there is no lower-bound constraint (nothing requires paddedInLength >= 512, i.e. inBlockIndex >= 1). paddedInLength = 0 is reachable through the public API because Sha256Bytes sets `sha.paddedInLength <== paddedInLength * 8;` (sha.circom:33) with no check on the byte length. With paddedInLength = 0 the length verifier passes, inBlockIndex = 0, and the selector index becomes -1 (= p-1). ItemAtIndex's guard `lessThan.in[0] <== index; lessThan.in[1] <== maxArrayLen; lessThan.out === 1;` (array.circom:25-28) is not effective because circomlib LessThan does not range-check its inputs: for index = p-1 the decomposed value `(index + 2^n - maxArrayLen) mod p = 2^n - maxArrayLen - 1` fits in n+1 bits with top bit 0, so `lessThan.out === 1` is satisfied. Since no i in [0, maxBlocks) equals p-1, every IsEqual output is 0 and `out[k] <== arraySelectors[k].out` (sha.circom:196) is forced to 0 for all 256 bits, independent of the paddedIn data. I reproduced the exact field arithmetic (Num2Bits/LessThan/LessEqThan/ItemAtIndex) in a local script: for maxBlocks = 1, 4 and 16, paddedInLength=0 passes bitLengthVerifier, index=-1 passes the ItemAtIndex check, and the selected output is 0. The same wrap-around also lets paddedInLength = p-1 (which is a multiple of 512, since p mod 512 = 1) satisfy `bitLengthVerifier.out === 1` even though it exceeds maxBitLength, confirming the length bound at sha.circom:126-128 is not enforced. Impact: soundness break of the SHA256 primitive - a malicious prover can produce a valid witness whose hash output is 0x00..0 for arbitrary input, so any downstream check comparing sha.out to an expected hash (or relying on the digest being a real SHA256 state) can be satisfied without a real preimage.

review_queue.evidence: Sha256General/Sha256Partial derive inBlockIndex from an unbounded paddedInLength and feed inBlockIndex-1 into ItemAtIndex, whose LessThan lacks a range check. Same comparator/selector soundness defect as the expected line-126 sink.

finding.title: Asymmetric public key misclassified as HMAC secret allows token forgery (algorithm confusion)
finding.evidence: detectPublicKeyAlgorithms decides key type with ^-anchored regexes: privateKeyPemMatcher=/^-----BEGIN(?: (RSA|EC|ENCRYPTED))? PRIVATE KEY-----/ (line 128) and publicKeyPemMatcher=/^-----BEGIN(?: (RSA))? PUBLIC KEY-----/ (line 126). If the configured key has any leading byte before the PEM header (leading whitespace/newline/BOM/control char, common for multi-line env vars, heredocs, or BOM-prefixed files), publicKeyPemMatch is null and key.includes(publicKeyX509CertMatcher) is false, so line 133 returns hsAlgorithms (the 'plain secret' fallback). I confirmed this classification locally: a clean PEM classifies as parse-pem, but '\n'+PUBLIC KEY and ' '+'PUBLIC KEY' both classify as hsAlgorithms. The verifier then calls prepareKeyOrSecret(key, availableAlgorithms[0]===hsAlgorithms[0]) at src/verifier.js:350, wrapping the public key bytes with createSecretKey. Because checkAreCompatibleAlgorithms (src/verifier.js:17-29) only requires the intersection of expected/actual to be non-empty, an operator who sets algorithms:['RS256','HS256'] (or leaves algorithms unset but the key region already includes HS via a sibling verifier) accepts the HS256 path. verifySignature (src/crypto.js:282-284) then validates the token with createHmac(alg, key) over the same public-key bytes. finding.title: SHA-256 length/padding constraints are not enforced, allowing forged hash outputs
finding.evidence: In Sha256General the message length and block index are derived from prover-controlled witnesses with hints rather than being fully bound to the input message. Line 110 (`inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9);`) uses the non-constraining hint operator, and the only binding is line 111 (`paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512;`). `paddedInLength` remains a free signal, so this equality merely defines `inBlockIndex` as `paddedInLength/512` (unique and invertible since gcd(512,p)=1); it does not establish that `paddedInLength` is the true byte length of `paddedIn`, nor that `paddedIn` is a correctly SHA-256-padded message. The verification block that would have constrained the block boundary is present only as comments (lines 113-122: floorVerifierUnder/floorVerifierOver are commented out), and lines 130-131 explicitly note that padding verification was intentionally removed from the circuit. The block selector then consumes the unverified value at line 195 (`arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1;`) and emits the compression output for that block at line 196, with the same pattern repeated in Sha256Partial (lines 233-234, 292-293). Because `paddedIn[maxBitLength]` is a fully free input array that is only width-checked via Num2Bits in Sha256Bytes/Sha256BytesPartial (lines 26-33, 58-64), an attacker who supplies the witness can choose arbitrary 512-bit block contents and an arbitrary `paddedInLength`/`inBlockIndex` pair. The circuit then returns the genuine SHA-256 compression output of the attacker-chosen block while the surrounding application treats `out` as the hash of the claimed padded message; the in-circuit constraints never tie the two together. Any verifier that relies on this component to prove that `out` is the hash of a properly padded message of length `paddedInLength` (e.g. hashing email/DKIM content before external padding checks) is therefore bypassable. Protections that would have closed this (the commented-out `floorVerifier` components and in-circuit padding checks) are inactive, so the missing constraint is reachable in the shipped component with only attacker-controlled prover inputs.

finding.title: Unvalidated block index lets prover force SHA256 output to all zeros (soundness break)
finding.evidence: Attacker-controlled signal input `paddedInLength` (lines 97/219) is tied to the block index on lines 110-111: `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9); paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512;`. Circomlib `LessThan(n)` only constrains `in[0]+2^n-in[1]` to fit in n+1 bits; it never bit-range-checks `index`, and field arithmetic is mod p. Choosing `paddedInLength` so that `inBlockIndex-1` is out of `[0,maxBlocks-1]` but close to p (e.g. inBlockIndex=0 giving index=p-1, or other near-p values) makes `index + 2^n - maxArrayLen` wrap to a small value, so `lessThan.out === 1` passes even though the index exceeds the array bound. The selector `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1` (line 195) then matches no entry, and `out <== calcTotal.sum` (array.circom line 45) is the sum of `eqs[i].out*in[i]`, which are all zero. finding.title: Unvalidated nb_blocks in argon2i_32 under-allocates work_area leading to heap overflow / NULL deref
finding.evidence: argon2i_32(nb_blocks, ...) copies the caller value into config.nb_blocks (line 328) and sizes the scratch buffer as work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * 1024) (line 345) without enforcing monocypher.h's documented contract 'nb_blocks >= 8 * nb_lanes' (nb_lanes is hard-coded to 1 at line 330) and without checking the malloc result before use (line 347). In monocypher.c, crypto_argon2 computes lane_size = (config.nb_blocks / config.nb_lanes / 4) * 4 (lines 752-754) and then unconditionally fills the first two blocks of every lane: 'FOR_T(u32, l, 0, config.nb_lanes) FOR_T(u32, i, 0, 2) { ... load64_le_buf(blocks[l * lane_size + i].a, hash_area, 128); }' (lines 776-782). When the caller passes nb_blocks == 1, segment_size/lane_size round down to 0, so the allocation is a single 1024-byte block, yet the C code writes blocks[0] and blocks[1], a 128-byte heap overflow past the malloc'd region. nb_blocks == 0 makes malloc(0) succeed with a minimal/null pointer while the same two-block write still occurs. Independently, a very large nb_blocks makes malloc fail; the unchecked NULL is then dereferenced/written by crypto_argon2 (initial fill and the final ZERO(p, 128 * nb_blocks) at line 915), giving an attacker-controlled null-pointer write / crash (DoS). The Python layer's _validate_u32 only bounds lengths fed to Argon2 inputs, never nb_blocks, so this argument reaches the unsafe operations unchecked.

finding.title: Double-drop in ThinVec::clear() when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: clear() does `unsafe { ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..]); self.set_len(0); }` (lines 1082-1087). The length is reset only *after* all elements are dropped, so it is not panic-safe: if `drop_in_place` unwinds (any element's `Drop::drop` panics — attacker-influenced for generic T), line 1085 (`set_len(0)`) never runs. The ThinVec still reports its old length (the PoC's `v.len()` stayed 3), so the already-dropped elements remain logically live. When the same vector is later dropped/cleared/iterated, those elements are dropped a second time (double free / double drop = UB, memory corruption). Reachable from entirely safe user code calling `v.clear()` on a `ThinVec<T>`. Upstream thin-vec 0.2.16 RELEASES.md records exactly this: "Fix two double-drop issues with ThinVec::clear() and ThinVec::into_iter() when the Drop implementation of the item panics", and 0.2.21 fixes it with a DropGuard that decrements len on unwind (confirming the target 0.2.15 code is the vulnerable form).

finding.title: Double-drop in IntoIter::drop when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: IntoIter::drop (lines 2539-2556) runs `let mut vec = mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new()); ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..]); vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)`. The zeroing of `vec.len` (line 2548) is the last statement and is skipped if `drop_in_place` (line 2547) unwinds because an element's `Drop::drop` panics. During unwinding the local `vec` goes out of scope and its own `Drop` runs again, re-dropping the elements in `this.start..` that were already (partially) dropped, i.e. a double-drop of live values (UB / double free). Partly-consumed iterators are the normal case: `into_iter(); it.next()` moves one element out, leaving `start>0`, then dropping `it` triggers the path. Reachable from safe code, and fixed upstream together with clear() per the 0.2.16 release notes (a DropGuard zeroing the length on unwind was added in 0.2.21).

finding.title: Unbounded BLAKE2b key length causes stack buffer overflow
finding.evidence: blake2b() forwards the caller-supplied key to crypto_blake2b_keyed(hash, len(hash), key, len(key), ...) at line 281 without enforcing any key-size bound, and Blake2b.__init__ does the same at line 297 (crypto_blake2b_keyed_init(&self._ctx, ..., key, len(key))). In monocypher.c, crypto_blake2b_keyed_init does `u8 key_block[128] = {0}; COPY(key_block, key, key_size);`, i.e. it copies key_size bytes into a fixed 128-byte stack buffer. Monocypher only supports keys up to 64 bytes; passing a key longer than 128 bytes writes past key_block and corrupts the stack (saved registers/return address), giving memory corruption that can be escalated to code execution. The wrapper performs no len(key) validation (contrast the explicit checks added for hidden/curve/seed elsewhere), so any code path that derives a BLAKE2b MAC key from untrusted data reaches the overflow.

finding.title: Missing length validation on fixed-size crypto inputs causes out-of-bounds reads
finding.evidence: signature_check() passes the caller-supplied signature and public_key straight to crypto_eddsa_check(signature, public_key, message, len(message)) at line 429 without validating their lengths. monocypher.c declares these parameters as const uint8_t signature[64] and public_key[32] and unconditionally reads exactly 64 and 32 bytes; Cython converts a Python bytes object to a raw pointer with no size check, so a short (e.g. empty or 1-byte) signature/public_key causes reads past the end of the buffer. Signature/public_key are the classic attacker-controlled inputs to a verification API. The same missing-validation root cause appears in unlock() line 199 (attacker-supplied mac forwarded to crypto_aead_unlock, which reads mac[16]), key_exchange() line 375 (attacker-supplied their_public_key read as 32 bytes by crypto_x25519), and lock()/unlock() key/nonce handling at lines 181/199, while elligator_map/elligator_rev/elligator_key_pair do validate. Reading adjacent heap memory out of bounds can disclose unrelated data or crash the process.

finding.title: Double free/use-after-free in ThinVec::clear when an element destructor panics
finding.evidence: ThinVec::clear (src/lib.rs:1082) runs ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..]) at line 1084 and only afterwards resets the length via self.set_len(0) at line 1085. The 0.2.16 fix wraps drop_in_place in a DropGuard that calls set_len(0) during unwinding; this 0.2.15 code has no such guard. finding.title: Unbounded paddedInLength underflows block index and forces SHA256 output to zero
finding.evidence: In Sha256General (and identically Sha256Partial, line 292) the number of processed blocks is taken from the prover-supplied length: line 110 `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9)` with the only constraints being line 111 `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` and the upper-bound check LessEqThan at lines 125-128. There is no lower-bound/nonzero constraint (and Sha256Bytes/Sha256BytesPartial only pass `paddedInLength * 8` through), so a prover can set paddedInLength = 0, which satisfies all constraints with inBlockIndex = 0. Line 195 then computes the ItemAtIndex selector index as `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1`, which in the BN254 field wraps 0-1 to p-1 (21888242871839275222246405745257275088548364400416034343698204186575808495616). ItemAtIndex's guard (array.circom lines 25-28, a LessThan built on Num2Bits inside circomlib/comparators.circom) assumes index < 2^bitLength; for index = p-1 its internal value `index + 2^n - maxArrayLen` reduces mod p to `2^n - maxArrayLen - 1`, whose bit n is always 0, so `lessThan.out === 1` is satisfied even though p-1 is far larger than maxArrayLen. No IsEqual in the loop matches p-1, so calcTotal.sum = 0 and every bit of `out` (line 196) is forced to 0 regardless of paddedIn. Required configuration: any instance where maxBitLength % 512 == 0 (asserted at line 90/213). Impact: an attacker supplying paddedInLength = 0 and arbitrary paddedIn gets a valid, satisfiable witness proving the hash gadget outputs an all-zero hash, breaking the soundness/binding of the SHA256 circuit (integrity violation). Confirmed with a field-accurate simulation of num2bits/LessThan/ItemAtIndex (poc_field_sim.py): for maxBlocks=2 the legitimate length 512 gives index 0 and the correct block output, while paddedInLength 0 gives index p-1, passes the range check, and yields output 0.

finding.title: Unconstrained paddedInLength/block index lets prover force all-zero SHA256 output

Line 195 then computes `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1` and feeds that value into ItemAtIndex (array.circom:25-28), whose LessThan-based bound is only sound for operands that fit in bitLength bits; index is never bit-constrained. With index ≡ 2^n - maxBlocks - d (mod p), lessThan.out===1 while no i in [0,maxBlocks) equals index, so all eqs[i].out are 0, calcTotal.sum is 0, and every out[k] is 0 (line 196). finding.title: ItemAtIndex accepts an out-of-range index and returns 0
finding.evidence: `LessThan(bitLength)` (line 25) evaluates in[0]+2^n-in[1] through Num2Bits(n+1) and outputs 1-bit[n]; it is sound only if both in[0] and in[1] are < 2^n. The constant maxArrayLen fits in bitLength bits, but the attacker-controlled `index` in[0] (bound at line 26) is never range-constrained to bitLength bits. Choosing index = p - d with 1 <= d <= 2^n - maxArrayLen causes in[0]+2^n-in[1] to wrap mod p to 2^n - maxArrayLen - d < 2^n, so lessThan.out === 1 (line 28) despite index >= maxArrayLen. Then no eqs[i] matches, no IsEqual output is 1, calcTotal.sum remains 0, and out = 0 (line 45) instead of being constrained. Reached from sha.circom:195/292 where index = inBlockIndex - 1 selects the SHA256 compression block, this returns an all-zero hash for any message.
